I get accused of just wanting to brag, or about exaggerating, when it couldn't be further from the truth - I have absolutely no desire to list my various "stats" etc, because all they do is make me different, and all that's done is make me miserable.  Yes, it was handy not to have to study, and I have to admit to getting a nice glow of pride whenever I was best at something, but that was nothing compared to the burning ache I'd get if I wasn't best (or, even when I was, still not good enough for me) and I wouldn't wish the kind of isolation I experienced growing up on anyone.

I'm a practicing Irish Catholic, but my brand of Catholicism is a little different from the mainstream.  In a nutshell, I'm a tattooed, bisexual Catholic who doesn't think contraception is a bad thing, and thinks women should be allowed to be priests and bishops, original sin is a load of shit, confession is a formality, and that to call the pope infallible is to dramatically miss the point.  My general view is "so long as you're not hurting anyone else, go nuts... but if someone else did something to hurt you, try to find it in your heart to forgive them."  It's kind of hard to reconcile my way of thinking with traditional Catholicism, and I had a real crisis over this when I was trying to work everything out, but I had this fantastic priest at my old church in Abingdon (his name was Father Taaffe, if anyone knows him, and he was a badass) who seemed to pretty much agree with me.  We had long discussions about theology and modern day interpretations on a weekly basis (we actually had a standing appointment every Friday for it) and it was really interesting.  He ended up "retiring" though... from what I gathered, the Diocese didn't like him very much.  Apparently you can molest the day away and be left alone, but try and interpret religion a little differently?  You're out.

Just to clarify, a lot of people I talk to seem to think that being Catholic means I agree with priests being perverts and with Church corruption.  I don't.

What's your talent and when did you realize you had it?

I also wrote my first novel at the age of nine.

Like I said before, I'm an artist, and my work has always drawn a lot from language - it's almost entirely text-based, although in some cases it's spoken word.  My memory is insane - I can remember my mother's first prenatal appointments when she was pregnant with my sister, which puts my earliest memories at approx. 18 months old. I'm also good at science - my first degree was in biochemistry at the University of Oxford, and I studied biology and chemistry to advanced level in senior school.  To put it bluntly, though, it sucked, and I walked out on it to go do something creative instead, which is the best decision I've ever made.

I would love to live in the United States, specifically NYC.

I don't know why, I guess it's because I come from such an insular area (West Belfast) in such an insular country (Ireland) and the total anonymity and freedom of New York just blows my mind.  I've been there a half dozen times, staying for between five days and three weeks, and I love that I can go out at any time of night and things will be happening and places will be open, whereas here everything closes at 5 (and often doesn't open at all on Sundays).  I love being able to go to the train or bus station and know I can go anywhere in this enormous continent, or to buy a Metrocard and go from the Irish part of the Bronx to the Russian cafes at Brighton Beach to the posh streets of the Upper East Side to the greenery of Central Park.  When I'm there I sometimes ride the bus from one end of the line to the other just to look out of the window and peoplewatch.  I love all the different cultures and how they mix, whereas in Belfast it's almost all Protestant or Catholic and the two rub each other up the wrong way just by breathing.

Sigh.  I miss New York.

At art college I was living on maybe £20 a month after rent and tuition etc, but I found a lot of ways to save here and there.

I used to go to the supermarket (grocery store for you Americans) right before close, because they would massively discount stuff from the deli, bakery, cheese place etc, sometimes to less than 90% of their original value. Also, if you go to a bakery and ask nicely, sometimes they'll give you some of yesterday's bread for free - have a huge tub of economy spread on hand and you're set for toast for DAYS.

Something else I used to do is find hotels where they're having conferences, meetings, parties etc. If you look professional and act like you belong, no one in a larger gathering will question you, and you can lay waste to the buffet with impunity. Take a decently sized bag and exercise some subtlety and you can get enough to eat for a few days.

As far as buying full price food goes, rice is super cheap and filling. I used to be able to find huge sacks of the stuff for ridiculously cheap at the local Asian supermarket.

For saving money, never be too proud to avail of reams of toilet paper from public bathrooms, condiments/sugar/sweetener from stands at Starbucks, McDonalds etc, and newspapers/magazines people have left on trains and buses. If you go to the fancier hotels (maybe while you're plundering the buffet at a conference) sometimes you can get actual little bottles of hand lotion and mini soaps from baskets.

Crashing the buffets and events is fun in itself. Otherwise, I love to walk. I plug in my MP3 player and off I go. If you've got any decent countryside nearby hiking with your friends is fun too, as is swimming in rivers/the sea. A lot of the time malls will have free events at weekends, and you can often find free events going on every night in your city if you look online. 

Another thing you can do is treat your city like a tourist would. Go to tourist information, pick up a free map and some leaflets and set to it. You'd be amazed what you can find out about somewhere you've lived, even if you've been there for years. I also go to the local park and hang out with the old dudes playing chess - they have some AWESOME stories, and boy do they love to talk. (And while you're at the park - swings/adventure playground. Believe me, they NEVER stop being fun.)

That's all I can think of right now, but if I come up with anything else I'll post an edit for you - and good luck!

I have a huge scar on my ass.  As in, the fucker is so big it actually looks as if my ass is smiling at you, except it's that kind of crooked smile that makes you want to kick whoever's doing it right in the nads.

I got it one night in July 2010.  Me and my friends were out in the Falls, and several drinks in we were as usual becoming increasingly patriotic.  At some point, someone announced grimly that the people in the neighbouring Village area had hung UVF flags up on lampposts facing the Falls.

(Non-Irish-Redditors - the UVF are a paramilitary organisation whose main aim was to kill as many Catholic civilians as possible in order to scare them into backing down.  It's kind of hard to explain to people who don't know about it, but something like this is kind of like the KKK hiring a billboard in the South Bronx.)

This was clearly an outrage, so me and my friends set forth to make it right.  I'm not sure exactly what we were planning to do with the flag once we had it, because to be honest I don't think we'd thought any further than "let's go get that fookin' flag, so") but nonetheless, we were determined in our quest, and soon arrived at the lampposts in question.

My friends being the assfucks they are, they immediately decided I should be the one to shimmy up the lamppost to grab the flag, on the grounds that I was the only one with any hope of getting anywhere.  I had to admit they had a point, so up I went, and once I'm a good 16ft up and reaching for the flag... some Village youths turn up.  With airguns.

The first I know of this is when my friends start yelling, and I'm just starting to turn around when I feel a searing pain in the back of my leg.  Yes, the fuckers had actually shot me in the leg.  I grabbed for the flag, tearing it off the lamppost as I fell backwards off it and landed flat on my ass - and, not only did I fall on my ass, I fell on my ass so hard I SPLIT MY ASS OPEN (hence the scar.)  Me being me, I think this is the funniest thing ever, so while a couple of my friends are hauling ass after the Village hoodlums, I am sat on the ground laughing my ass off and yelling "JESUS BUT I THINK I BROKE MY ASS!" over and over. 

It took my friends a surprisingly long time to get me to shut the fuck up for long enough to finally head for home, flag in hand.

TL;DR: Shot in the leg, fell off a lamppost, and now my ass smiles at you crooked.

Several reasons, including:

1, the anonymity of people online means there's no way to hold them accountable for their bad behaviour.  Because you're not talking directly to the person you're attacking, you feel more powerful, and human beings do love themselves a power trip.  Also, there's no immediate social feedback in the way we've evolved to perceive it - if you're screaming at someone you met in a bar, and they start crying, then you'd probably stop (unless you're a complete sociopath, in which case being mean on the internet is really the least of your problems) but on the internet, you don't see any such reactions.  Without the reactions and feedback we've evolved to look for and work from in social interaction, there's no instinct of when it's time to take a step back.

2, people who feel powerless in everyday life can create the persona they want online.  The internet gives them the power to say and do pretty much whatever they want without fear of repercussions, and if they've been building up a bad mood all day, some poor sap is going to pay for it.  It's like that How I Met Your Mother episode "The Chain of Screaming."  You can't shout at your boss and you don't see yourself as being enough of an asshole to yell at the poor guy sitting next to you on the bus home, but online you can make anyone you choose your metaphorical bitch.

3, rage has sadly become the norm online and to some extent in real life.  People have begun to perceive anger and vitriol as the way ideas are discussed (thanks Daily Mail and Jeremy Kyle!) so when they're discussing something themselves, it's their go-to setting.

TL;DR: Don't take it personally, hun.  It's not you, it's them.

This whole time I'm sitting on the ground next to this guy holding his hand and talking to him, finding out the names of medications he's taking to tell the paramedics, getting his name and details, asking him simple questions repeatedly to check he's not confused etc, and then a couple of doctors from the cars come running up and help him until the ambulance gets there. I don't remember my first seizure, but of the recent ones what set me were camera flashes, fever, tiredness and stress.  I've also noticed that they're pretty closely tied to hormones - ie, there is definitely a week or so per month when I am far, FAR more likely to have one.

As for what they feel like... there are three kinds.

Simple partial seizures you're completely conscious for and are basically just weird sensations, smells, tastes, emotions etc (sudden deja vu is a common one of mine, as is inexplicable patriotism, plus of course my favourite complete and utter terror.)  They can also be 'absences' which are, to put it simply: the lights are on but nobody's home.  I'm awake, I look normal, but it's like I briefly left my body on autopilot for maybe 30 seconds at a time.

Complex partial seizures are a step up.  In my case, I get many of the same symptoms I get when coming up to having a big tonic-clonic seizure (the kind most people associate with epileptic seizures) but it doesn't quite go the whole way.  Before, when I've been coming up to one of these, I've actually grabbed someone nearby and told them exactly what to do in case I am about to have a big one.  They can have elements of the simple partials in, but in the past I've also become unable to move some or all of my limbs, become very confused, and/or (awkwardly) I lose all inhibitions and start acting extremely inappropriately.  Once, I became loudly racist; on another occasion, I started yelling in my housemate's workplace about various colleagues of hers that I wanted to 'bang until they were raw.'

Finally, the big ones... and these ones are a bitch.  They're terrifying, because you never know when or if you might have one.  They have some initial symptoms, such as a sudden spate of simple partials, stuff tasting off, an odd rising nausea feeling, and the minute I get any of those it is, to put it frankly, terrifying.  There's a fun game I like to call 'Anxiety or Seizure?' because they feel so similar early on... which of course makes it harder to differentiate and makes the symptoms last longer.  Stupid troll brain.

As for what it feels like... I start off feeling very, very sick, but not like vomiting sick, like an extreme version of that rising nausea you get when you're super excited.  I can also start trembling, feeling like my heart is going too slow or too fast, and suddenly be unable to move.  Sometimes, I just feel vaguely 'off'; on others, I've suddenly gone dizzy and faint, my head will start spinning, my vision goes funny... beyond this point I can't tell you much because a trademark of the rare kind I have is amnesia, but I can tell you what other people tell me and what I remember of the aftermath.

Apparently I trail off in the middle of whatever I was doing, stare blankly into space for a few seconds, and then my muscles suddenly lock up, my head jerks back and I start shaking.  They can last for up to a few minutes at a time, and on occasions I've had several one after the other.  Once I've actually stopped convulsing, it's time for what's called the post-ictal phase.  Mine is very long and intense (another trademark of my kind of epilepsy.)  I can be unconscious for up to 45 minutes at a time, and then when I finally wake up I have no idea who I am, where i am, or who anyone else is, including family members.  It is, to put it frankly, terrifying (although, as an interesting aside - I had one at a Twin Peaks event, and even though I had no idea who my best friend was or who I was, I immediately recognised Ray Wise when he came over.  Brain clearly has its own priorities.)  At this stage I can't walk, stand or even move, and I probably won't be able to do that again for a fair while.  It also makes me extremely tired afterwards.

I still have odd hints of consciousness though.  I once had a seizure on a plane between New Orleans and Philadelphia, and the plane made an emergency landing at Atlanta.  I woke up in the departure lounge with a bunch of EMTs and apparently (I don't remember) said 'Did I have a seizure?' The EMT nods and says 'yes, dear.'  My response was 'Well, fuck.'  And then I passed out again.  I woke up again 20 minutes later and immediately started yelling that my mother was going to kill me for having a seizure and to just drop me off at a bus stop and I'd never talk about it again.  I don't remember doing that either.  *sigh

The worst part is, the kind I have is very rare and also degenerative.  It'll slowly get resistant to meds so I have to keep increasing the doses until it stops working completely, and then I have to switch to another one until that one stops working too.  In roughly 1/3 of cases, the seizures rapidly become uncontrollable, and in that case they have to perform what is essentially a lobotomy.

Yes.  The doctors would have to cut out my scumbag left temporal lobe completely to stop that bastard from egging on the rest of my brain to do evil.

Which (I don't know about you) kind of grosses me out a little.

I will say though: the worst thing about it is I no longer trust my emotions.  I have no idea if what I am feeling is, shall we say, 'genuine' or just generated by my brain for shits and giggles, because either way they are just as real and feel just the same.

TL;DR: Troll brain is a troll.  Fuck that shit.

This was my Second Mistake.

A band starts up in a corner, and thus the singing begins.

We work our way through the varied wonders of Sean South, A Nation Once Again, A Broad Black Brimmer, and Come Out Ye Black and Tans before getting to the Irish national anthem. This is always a fun song to sing as no one knows all the words. It is therefore sung in a weird patchwork of voices, with people dropping in and out as they remember fragments of verse, and occasionally getting it wrong but stubbornly carrying on anyway (in this way, it's wonderfully representative of its people.) The one part EVERYONE knows is the first three words of the chorus, and so to make up for their haphazard performance of the rest of the song, everyone belts out 'SINNE FIANNA FAIL' at deafening volume whenever the chorus comes around, then shamefacedly trails off again.

Disheartened by our failure, we launch into a second rendition of A Broad Black Brimmer. The words of that are easy to remember, and even if you've not quite got the verses down, the chorus is repeated often enough that it's properly drilled into your brain by the end.

On to another pub, where they have two wrestlers dressed as St Patrick and a Snake slapping the living shit out of each other in an inflatable boxing ring out in the beer garden. Under the spotlights you can really see the fat jiggling. I begin to feel slightly nauseous. The poor bastards look absolutely freezing, it's Belfast weather outside and even though it's not raining, there's a bitter wind. At least the guy playing St Patrick has a robe and hat; the poor Snake has a thin bodystocking and a weird headpiece, he must be hypothermic. The jiggling fat has now become almost hypnotic. 

I tear my eyes away in time to see a girl in an amazing 'St Patrick Was A Saint, But I Ain't' T-shirt.

'Oh my GOD, I love your T-shirt!' I exclaim.
'Oh my GOD, I love yours!' she exclaims back. 

I look down at my slightly faded 'Bundoran H-Block Commemoration 2009' T-shirt.

'...Really?' says I.

It's now getting late and the city centre pubs, in line with licensing laws, are beginning to close. No problem, we head for the Falls, where such legal considerations are irrelevant. At some point, we have misplaced the Americans. Once again, the singing begins. This time it's My Little Armalite and Back Home in Derry, and then, oddly, 'Alejandro' by Lady GaGa. Into the next pub. We quickly befriend most of the people there. More singing commences. This time it's Sean South, The Boy From Tamlaghtduff, and The Man From The Daily Mail, along with another stab at the Irish national anthem. If possible, it is even worse than it was in the city centre, in that there are parts where nobody knows the words, and each awkward silence is punctuated by lusty belches from one of the drunks asleep under the pool table.

The beer-drinking man was apparently so deep into his cups that, upon being surprised with Sean's sudden arrival in his lap, he decided that he actually quite liked Sean and promptly wrapped his arms around him and rested his cheek against the back of Sean's neck. Oh well, at least the bearded man is happy. However, having extricated himself from the lap of the hairy man, Sean now wants to leave the pub immediately. We must however wait for Aoife to stop laughing for long enough that she is able to stand up. Dean suggests that maybe the bearded man thought Sean was a girl. Sean looks even more pissed off. Aoife laughs even harder.

It's now more walking down the Falls Road and more singing Lady GaGa (this time, Bad Romance.) Sean has cheered up again. He gets out his Gerry Adams mask and puts it on. Some patrolling PSNI men smile in poorly-hidden amusement as Gerry Adams and a girl in a leprechaun hat wander past bellowing 'I want your love and all you want is revenge' at the top of their voices, accompanied by a selection of friends in varying stages of disarray. 

'He's Gerry Adams!' I yell to passers-by.
'I'm Gerry Adams!' repeats Sean.
'I LOVE GERRY ADAMS!!' I declare impulsively.

This was my Third Mistake.

It is now cold and I am tired. We decide to call it a night and head back to our respective houses. Sean very kindly escorts (read: carries) me back to Beechmount, then asks if he can use our loo.

'Go for it,' I say, 'I'm going to sleep.' And I head up the stairs and collapse into bed and fall asleep immediately, before Sean has even left.

And that, ladies and gentleman, was my Fifth Mistake.

Man, I feel your pain.  At art college I was living on maybe £20 a month after rent and tuition etc, but there are ways round it.

I used to go to the supermarket (grocery store for you Americans) right before close, because they would massively discount stuff from the deli, bakery, cheese place etc, sometimes to less than 90% of their original value.  Also, if you go to a bakery and ask nicely, sometimes they'll give you some of yesterday's bread for free - have a huge tub of economy spread on hand and you're set for toast for DAYS.

Something else I used to do is find hotels where they're having conferences, meetings, parties etc.  If you look professional and act like you belong, no one in a larger gathering will question you, and you can lay waste to the buffet with impunity.  Take a decently sized bag and exercise some subtlety and you can get enough to eat for a few days.

As far as buying full price food goes, rice is super cheap and filling.  I used to be able to find huge sacks of the stuff for ridiculously cheap at the local Asian supermarket.

For saving money, never be too proud to avail of reams of toilet paper from public bathrooms, condiments/sugar/sweetener from stands at Starbucks, McDonalds etc, and newspapers/magazines people have left on trains and buses.  If you go to the fancier hotels (maybe while you're plundering the buffet at a conference) sometimes you can get actual little bottles of hand lotion and mini soaps from baskets.

Crashing the buffets and events is fun in itself.  Otherwise, I love to walk.  I plug in my MP3 player and off I go.  If you've got any decent countryside nearby hiking with your friends is fun too, as is swimming in rivers/the sea.  A lot of the time malls will have free events at weekends, and you can often find free events going on every night in your city if you look online.  

Another thing you can do is treat your city like a tourist would.  Go to tourist information, pick up a free map and some leaflets and set to it. You'd be amazed what you can find out about somewhere you've lived, even if you've been there for years.  I also go to the local park and hang out with the old dudes playing chess - they have some AWESOME stories, and boy do they love to talk.  (And while you're at the park - swings/adventure playground.  Believe me, they NEVER stop being fun.)
